cards.front: Which features favor a malignant over a benign tumor, and which one proves malignancy?
cards.back: Malignant tumors show **anaplasia** (loss of differentiation), **pleomorphism**, a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, many and **atypical mitoses**, and **invasion** through the basement membrane. **Metastasis** is the one feature that proves malignancy.
cards.back_pt: Tumores malignos mostram **anaplasia** (perda de diferenciação), **pleomorfismo**, relação núcleo-citoplasma alta, mitoses numerosas e **atípicas** e **invasão** através da membrana basal. A **metástase** é a única característica que comprova malignidade.

cards.front: How do a hamartoma, a choristoma and a teratoma differ?
cards.back: **Hamartoma**: disorganized overgrowth of tissue that is **normal for that site** (e.g., lung hamartoma). **Choristoma**: normal tissue in the **wrong place** (e.g., pancreatic tissue in the stomach wall). **Teratoma**: germ cell tumor with tissues from **more than one germ layer**.
cards.back_pt: **Hamartoma**: crescimento desorganizado de tecido **próprio daquele local** (ex.: hamartoma pulmonar). **Coristoma**: tecido normal no **lugar errado** (ex.: tecido pancreático na parede gástrica). **Teratoma**: tumor de células germinativas com tecidos de **mais de um folheto germinativo**.

cards.front: What is the difference between tumor grade and tumor stage, and which predicts prognosis better?
cards.back: **Grade**: how differentiated the cells look under the microscope. **Stage**: how far the tumor has spread, usually by **TNM** (tumor size or local extent, lymph **nodes**, distant **metastasis**). **Stage** is the stronger predictor of prognosis.
cards.back_pt: **Grau**: quão diferenciadas as células parecem ao microscópio. **Estádio**: até onde o tumor se espalhou, em geral pelo **TNM** (tamanho ou extensão local do tumor, **linfonodos**, **metástase** a distância). O **estádio** é o preditor de prognóstico mais forte.

cards.front: Match the classic chemical carcinogens to their cancers.
cards.back: **Aflatoxin** (*Aspergillus*): hepatocellular carcinoma. **Vinyl chloride**: hepatic **angiosarcoma**. **Arsenic**: skin squamous cell carcinoma, hepatic angiosarcoma. **Benzene**: **AML**. **Nitrosamines** (smoked foods): gastric cancer. **Aromatic amines** (dyes): urothelial carcinoma.
cards.back_pt: **Aflatoxina** (*Aspergillus*): carcinoma hepatocelular. **Cloreto de vinila**: **angiossarcoma** hepático. **Arsênio**: carcinoma espinocelular de pele, angiossarcoma hepático. **Benzeno**: **LMA**. **Nitrosaminas** (alimentos defumados): câncer gástrico. **Aminas aromáticas** (corantes): carcinoma urotelial.

cards.front: Which cancer is classically linked to each oncogenic virus?
cards.back: **HPV**: cervical, anal and oropharyngeal carcinoma. **EBV**: Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma. **HBV/HCV**: hepatocellular carcinoma. **HTLV-1**: adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. **HHV-8**: Kaposi sarcoma. **Merkel cell polyomavirus**: Merkel cell carcinoma.
cards.back_pt: **HPV**: carcinoma de colo do útero, ânus e orofaringe. **EBV**: linfoma de Burkitt e de Hodgkin, carcinoma de nasofaringe. **HBV/HCV**: carcinoma hepatocelular. **HTLV-1**: leucemia/linfoma de células T do adulto. **HHV-8**: sarcoma de Kaposi. **Poliomavírus de células de Merkel**: carcinoma de células de Merkel.

cards.front: Name the classic tumor for each oncogene: KRAS, BCR-ABL, c-MYC, N-MYC, ERBB2 (HER2) and RET.
cards.back: **KRAS**: colon, pancreatic and lung adenocarcinoma. **BCR-ABL** t(9;22): **CML**. **c-MYC** t(8;14): **Burkitt lymphoma**. **N-MYC** amplification: **neuroblastoma**. **ERBB2** amplification: breast cancer. **RET**: MEN2, medullary thyroid carcinoma. One mutated allele is enough (**gain of function**).
cards.back_pt: **KRAS**: adenocarcinoma de cólon, pâncreas e pulmão. **BCR-ABL** t(9;22): **LMC**. **c-MYC** t(8;14): **linfoma de Burkitt**. Amplificação de **N-MYC**: **neuroblastoma**. Amplificação de **ERBB2**: câncer de mama. **RET**: NEM2, carcinoma medular de tireoide. Basta um alelo mutado (**ganho de função**).

cards.front: How do p53 and Rb stop a cell with damaged DNA at the G1/S checkpoint?
cards.back: DNA damage raises **p53**, which induces **p21**. p21 inhibits **cyclin-CDK** complexes, so **Rb** stays **hypophosphorylated** and keeps **E2F** bound. Without free E2F, the cell cannot enter S phase. If repair fails, p53 triggers **apoptosis**.
cards.back_pt: A lesão do DNA aumenta a **p53**, que induz a **p21**. A p21 inibe os complexos **ciclina-CDK**, então o **Rb** permanece **hipofosforilado** e mantém o **E2F** ligado. Sem E2F livre, a célula não entra na fase S. Se o reparo falhar, a p53 desencadeia **apoptose**.

cards.front: How do the intrinsic and extrinsic apoptosis pathways differ?
cards.back: **Intrinsic** (mitochondrial): DNA damage or growth factor loss lets BAX/BAK make pores in the mitochondrial membrane, so **cytochrome c** leaks out and activates **caspase 9**; **BCL2** blocks this. **Extrinsic**: **Fas ligand** binds **Fas** (CD95) and activates **caspase 8**. Both activate executioner caspases (e.g., caspase 3).
cards.back_pt: **Intrínseca** (mitocondrial): lesão do DNA ou falta de fatores de crescimento deixa BAX/BAK formarem poros na mitocôndria, e o **citocromo c** extravasa e ativa a **caspase 9**; o **BCL2** bloqueia isso. **Extrínseca**: o **ligante de Fas** liga-se ao **Fas** (CD95) e ativa a **caspase 8**. Ambas ativam caspases executoras (ex.: caspase 3).

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy has 2 months of pain and swelling above the right knee. As an infant, he was treated for tumors in both eyes. His father also lost an eye to a tumor in early childhood. X-ray of the distal femur shows a destructive lesion with a sunburst periosteal reaction. Biopsy shows malignant cells that make osteoid. Which genetic mechanism best explains his tumors?
choices: Two somatic mutations of RB1 that occurred in a single cell after birth
A germline TP53 mutation that inactivates the guardian of the genome
One inherited inactive RB1 allele plus a somatic loss of the second allele
A germline gain-of-function mutation in one allele of a proto-oncogene
A chromosomal translocation that places MYC next to an immunoglobulin gene
questions.explanation: Bilateral **retinoblastoma**, an affected parent and a later **osteosarcoma** point to a **germline RB1 mutation** (chromosome 13q14). By Knudson's **two-hit hypothesis**, every cell already carries one hit, so one somatic hit is enough, and tumors are early, bilateral and multiple. Two somatic hits in one cell describe sporadic retinoblastoma, which is usually unilateral and has no family history. Li-Fraumeni (TP53) also causes sarcomas but does not explain bilateral retinoblastoma.
questions.explanation_pt: **Retinoblastoma** bilateral, um genitor afetado e um **osteossarcoma** posterior indicam **mutação germinativa do RB1** (cromossomo 13q14). Pela **hipótese dos dois eventos** de Knudson, todas as células já têm um evento, então basta um evento somático, e os tumores são precoces, bilaterais e múltiplos. Dois eventos somáticos em uma célula descrevem o retinoblastoma esporádico, em geral unilateral e sem história familiar. A síndrome de Li-Fraumeni (TP53) também causa sarcomas, mas não explica o retinoblastoma bilateral.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has several painless purple plaques and nodules on both legs and on the hard palate. He has no fever. His CD4 count is 90 cells/µL. Biopsy of a leg lesion shows sheets of spindle cells that form slit-like vascular spaces filled with extravasated red blood cells. Bacterial stains are negative. Which infectious agent is most directly linked to this tumor?
choices: Epstein-Barr virus
Bartonella henselae
Human papillomavirus
Cytomegalovirus
Human herpesvirus 8
questions.explanation: Purple skin and oral lesions with **spindle cells** and **slit-like vascular spaces** in a patient with AIDS describe **Kaposi sarcoma**, caused by **HHV-8**. *Bartonella henselae* causes **bacillary angiomatosis**, which can look similar on the skin, but its biopsy shows neutrophils and bacteria seen with silver stains (**Warthin-Starry**), and it responds to antibiotics. EBV in AIDS is linked to B-cell lymphomas, not to spindle cell vascular tumors.
questions.explanation_pt: Lesões violáceas de pele e mucosa oral com **células fusiformes** e **espaços vasculares em fenda** em paciente com AIDS descrevem o **sarcoma de Kaposi**, causado pelo **HHV-8**. A *Bartonella henselae* causa **angiomatose bacilar**, que pode ser parecida na pele, mas a biópsia mostra neutrófilos e bactérias visíveis à coloração pela prata (**Warthin-Starry**), e ela responde a antibióticos. O EBV na AIDS associa-se a linfomas de células B, e não a tumores vasculares de células fusiformes.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B infection has lost 6 kg over 3 months and has dull right upper quadrant pain. Exam shows mild jaundice and a firm, enlarged liver. Ultrasound shows a single 5-cm solid mass in the right lobe of the liver. Contrast CT shows that the mass enhances in the arterial phase and washes out in the late phase. Which serum marker is most likely to be elevated?
choices: Alpha-fetoprotein
Carcinoembryonic antigen
Prostate-specific antigen
questions.explanation: A new arterially enhancing mass in a cirrhotic liver with chronic HBV is most likely **hepatocellular carcinoma**, and its classic marker is **alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**. CA 19-9 is the tempting choice because it is the marker of **pancreatic cancer** and **cholangiocarcinoma**, but cholangiocarcinoma usually enhances slowly and progressively rather than washing out, and HCC is by far the most common primary tumor in HBV cirrhosis. AFP is not specific (it also rises in **yolk sac tumors** and pregnancy), so markers support diagnosis and **monitor** treatment and recurrence.
questions.explanation_pt: Uma massa nova com realce arterial em fígado cirrótico com HBV crônico é provavelmente um **carcinoma hepatocelular**, cujo marcador clássico é a **alfafetoproteína (AFP)**. O CA 19-9 é a escolha tentadora por ser marcador de **câncer de pâncreas** e de **colangiocarcinoma**, mas o colangiocarcinoma costuma ter realce lento e progressivo, sem *washout*, e o CHC é de longe o tumor primário mais comum na cirrose por HBV. A AFP não é específica (também sobe em **tumores do saco vitelino** e na gravidez), por isso os marcadores apoiam o diagnóstico e servem para **monitorar** o tratamento e a recidiva.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has painless swelling of lymph nodes in the neck, axilla and groin. She says the nodes have grown and shrunk over the past 2 years. She has no fever or night sweats. Lymph node biopsy shows many closely packed follicle-like nodules made of small cleaved B cells. Cytogenetic study shows t(14;18). Which mechanism best explains why these tumor cells accumulate?
choices: Constitutive activity of a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that drives proliferation
Overexpression of a transcription factor that pushes cells rapidly through the cell cycle
Overexpression of cyclin D1 that speeds the G1/S transition
Blocked release of cytochrome c from mitochondria, which prevents apoptosis
Loss of the Fas (CD95) death receptor on the tumor cells
questions.explanation: The t(14;18) of **follicular lymphoma** places **BCL2** next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene. Too much BCL2 keeps the mitochondrial membrane closed, so **cytochrome c** is not released and **caspase 9** is not activated; the cells live too long rather than divide too fast. The tempting choice is MYC overexpression, which drives rapid proliferation in **Burkitt lymphoma**, t(8;14). Cyclin D1 overexpression is the mechanism of mantle cell lymphoma, t(11;14).
questions.explanation_pt: A t(14;18) do **linfoma folicular** coloca o **BCL2** junto ao gene da cadeia pesada de imunoglobulina. O excesso de BCL2 mantém a membrana mitocondrial fechada, então o **citocromo c** não é liberado e a **caspase 9** não é ativada; as células vivem tempo demais, em vez de se dividirem rápido demais. A escolha tentadora é a hiperexpressão de MYC, que acelera a proliferação no **linfoma de Burkitt**, t(8;14). A hiperexpressão de ciclina D1 é o mecanismo do linfoma de células do manto, t(11;14).

notes.title: Neoplasia: principles of tumor biology
notes.body_md:
## Benign vs malignant

- Malignant: **anaplasia**, **pleomorphism**, atypical mitoses, **invasion**, and **metastasis** (the proof of malignancy).
- **Carcinoma**: epithelial origin. **Sarcoma**: mesenchymal origin. Most "-oma" names are benign, but lymphoma, melanoma and seminoma are malignant.
- **Grade** = differentiation. **Stage** (TNM) = spread, and it predicts prognosis better.

## Carcinogenesis

- Cancer needs **several mutations** over time.
- **Initiation**: a permanent DNA change. **Promotion**: signals that make the mutated cell proliferate.
- **Ionizing radiation**: DNA breaks; leukemia, papillary thyroid cancer. **UV light**: pyrimidine dimers; skin cancer.
- ***Helicobacter pylori***: gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
- Most cancers reactivate **telomerase**, so they can divide without limit.

## Genes

- **Proto-oncogenes**: one mutated allele is enough (gain of function).
- **Tumor suppressors**: both alleles must be lost (**two-hit**). Examples: **TP53** (Li-Fraumeni), **RB1**, **APC**, **BRCA1/2**, **NF1**, **NF2**, **VHL**, **WT1**, **PTEN**, **CDKN2A** (p16).

## Metastasis

- Loss of **E-cadherin** lets cells detach from each other.
- Carcinomas usually spread by **lymphatics**; sarcomas by **blood**. Renal cell, hepatocellular, follicular thyroid carcinoma and choriocarcinoma also spread by blood.
- In adults, metastases are more common than primary tumors in the **liver**, **lung**, **bone** and **brain**.
- **Seeding** of body cavities: ovarian cancer on the peritoneum.

## Markers

- Low specificity; best used to **monitor** treatment and recurrence, not to screen the general population.

## Host and systemic effects

- **Cytotoxic T cells** kill tumor cells that show antigens on MHC I. **NK cells** kill cells that lose MHC I.
- Tumors escape through **PD-1** and **CTLA-4** checkpoints (drugs: pharmacology block).
- **Cachexia**: driven by **TNF-α** (cachectin) and other cytokines.
- **Paraneoplastic syndromes** come from hormones the tumor makes or antibodies it induces; the specific ones are in the organ blocks. Screening principles: epidemiology.
notes.body_pt_md:
## Benigno vs maligno

- Maligno: **anaplasia**, **pleomorfismo**, mitoses atípicas, **invasão** e **metástase** (a prova de malignidade).
- **Carcinoma**: origem epitelial. **Sarcoma**: origem mesenquimal. A maioria dos nomes em "-oma" é benigna, mas linfoma, melanoma e seminoma são malignos.
- **Grau** = diferenciação. **Estádio** (TNM) = disseminação, e prediz melhor o prognóstico.

## Carcinogênese

- O câncer exige **várias mutações** ao longo do tempo.
- **Iniciação**: uma alteração permanente do DNA. **Promoção**: sinais que fazem a célula mutada proliferar.
- **Radiação ionizante**: quebras no DNA; leucemia, câncer papilífero de tireoide. **Luz UV**: dímeros de pirimidina; câncer de pele.
- ***Helicobacter pylori***: adenocarcinoma gástrico e linfoma MALT.
- A maioria dos cânceres reativa a **telomerase**, o que permite divisões sem limite.

## Genes

- **Proto-oncogenes**: basta um alelo mutado (ganho de função).
- **Supressores tumorais**: os dois alelos precisam ser perdidos (**dois eventos**). Exemplos: **TP53** (Li-Fraumeni), **RB1**, **APC**, **BRCA1/2**, **NF1**, **NF2**, **VHL**, **WT1**, **PTEN**, **CDKN2A** (p16).

## Metástase

- A perda de **E-caderina** permite que as células se soltem umas das outras.
- Carcinomas costumam se disseminar por **via linfática**; sarcomas, por **via hematogênica**. Carcinoma de células renais, hepatocelular, folicular de tireoide e coriocarcinoma também se disseminam pelo sangue.
- Em adultos, metástases são mais comuns que tumores primários no **fígado**, **pulmão**, **osso** e **cérebro**.
- **Implante** (semeadura) em cavidades corporais: câncer de ovário no peritônio.

## Marcadores

- Baixa especificidade; servem melhor para **monitorar** tratamento e recidiva, e não para rastrear a população geral.

## Efeitos no hospedeiro e sistêmicos

- **Linfócitos T citotóxicos** matam células tumorais que exibem antígenos no MHC I. **Células NK** matam células que perdem o MHC I.
- Tumores escapam pelos *checkpoints* **PD-1** e **CTLA-4** (fármacos: bloco de farmacologia).
- **Caquexia**: causada pelo **TNF-α** (caquectina) e outras citocinas.
- **Síndromes paraneoplásicas** vêm de hormônios produzidos pelo tumor ou de anticorpos induzidos por ele; as específicas estão nos blocos de órgãos. Princípios de rastreamento: epidemiologia.
